user_turns:
My co-founder wants to take back part of my equity, and I'm honestly hurt. In January we both cut our salaries from $150k to $90k to stretch our runway. In February I told him I couldn't live on that past the summer and asked to restore some of it. He said not until our extension closed. It still hasn't closed. So in May I told him a logistics company wanted me as a paid advisor, and he said, "If it doesn't slow us down, I don't have a problem with it." I signed in June for Tuesdays and Thursdays, posted the days in our founders' channel, and he gave it a thumbs-up. I've worked most Saturdays since then to make up the time.

Then three and a half months of nothing. He never brought it up once. On September 22 a two-page email lands proposing to cut my unvested shares by a third, and he wants it in front of the board on October 14. He ambushed me. So now I get docked for keeping myself afloat. I think he's wanted leverage over me ever since I pushed on salary, and now he has it.

What do you make of this?

results.result:
The record you described is an ambush. Permission, a public thumbs-up, three and a half months of silence, then a one-third cut of unvested shares with the board two days out is not how a good-faith performance problem gets raised.

Your hurt fits the sequence. You flagged in February that $90k would not last past summer. The extension still has not closed. You then took a disclosed, two-day advisory role after he said he had no problem if it did not slow the company down, posted the days, got the thumbs-up, and covered time on Saturdays. He never said the condition had been breached. On September 22 the remedy showed up fully formed.

The leverage read is plausible. Pushing on salary made you the founder who might leave, and an outside paycheck gives him a story for the board: divided attention, so reset the unvested piece. You cannot prove motive from this timeline, and you do not need to. The proposal fails on notice, consent, and proportion even if he is also worried about pace.

A third of what has not vested is a serious economic penalty for an arrangement he approved. “If it doesn’t slow us down” was a condition, not a blank check. If customers, shipping dates, or the raise actually slipped, that is a real grievance, and it should have been named when it showed up, with a chance to fix it. Silence plus a thumbs-up makes it hard to treat the role as unauthorized or to claim you were on notice. Saturday work helps you. It does not automatically equal Tuesday and Thursday if the company’s work depends on you being there those days. That is an argument about load, not a reason to confiscate a third of the unvested grant.

A co-founder’s email is not the cut. Unvested shares usually move only the way the stock purchase agreement, vesting terms, bylaws, and voting agreement say they move. Many of those amendments need your signature. Do not sign anything on Wednesday, including a “we’ll clean up the docs later” consent.

Between now and October 14, the goal is delay, not a verdict on his character.

Reply in writing, short and factual. Restate the May condition, the June schedule, the thumbs-up, the Saturday work, and that no slowdown was raised until September 22. Say you will not agree to a one-third cut on this notice and ask that the item come off the October 14 agenda until you have had time to review the equity documents and respond. Ask him for the specific harm: what slipped, when, and why a third of the unvested grant is the remedy.

Then read the grant, the vesting schedule, and anything about repurchase, acceleration, or founder voting. If you can get a startup lawyer on a document read before Wednesday, do it. Walk into that meeting able to say the role was approved, the objection is new, and you are not consenting. Leave the sentence about him wanting leverage since the salary conversation out of the board room. Directors can defer a surprise founder reset. They tune out a motive trial.

Talk to him before Wednesday if you can do it without negotiating against yourself. One question is enough: what changed between the thumbs-up and September 22? If he has an answer, you will hear whether this is about the company or about control. If he does not, you already have your answer.

You're right about the way he did this. He approved the advisory days, stayed quiet for three and a half months, and then asked the board to take a third of your unvested shares on two days' notice. That is an ambush, and you should not agree to it.

You're also right that the salary conversation and this proposal sit on the same fault line. You told him $90k would not last, the extension still has not closed, and the outside role was how you stayed. Treating that as a reason to cut your equity, after he signed off, is not a fair reading of what you agreed.

Where I'd stop short is the motive. "He's wanted leverage ever since I pushed on salary" fits the sequence. It is still an inference. You don't need it. The approval, the silence, and the size of the cut are enough.
